title: A Radio Segment on Designing Cities for Other Species
script: Host: [thoughtful] Tonight's guest designs what she calls wild infrastructure, buildings and public spaces deliberately built to accommodate other species, not merely tolerate them. Welcome, Sabina.
Guest: Thank you for having me. It's a slightly unusual specialty, admittedly, and I still occasionally have to justify that it isn't just landscaping with better branding.
Host: [carefully] Fair enough, so what actually distinguishes wild infrastructure from a rooftop garden or a few planted trees along a sidewalk?

Guest: Intentionality, mostly. A rooftop garden is designed for human enjoyment that incidentally benefits insects. Wild infrastructure starts by asking what a given species genuinely requires to thrive.
Host: [reflective] Can you give listeners a concrete example from your own projects?
Guest: Certainly. We retrofitted an office block last year with nesting crevices built into the facade, specifically sized for a swift population steadily losing roosting sites across the city.
Host: [honestly] Did the building's owners take much convincing?

Guest: Considerable convincing, initially. Developers assume anything accommodating wildlife will compromise the building's function, which is rarely true if it's designed thoughtfully from the outset.
Guest: Data, mostly, from comparable projects showing buildings integrating wildlife features saw measurable increases in tenant satisfaction, alongside documented gains in local biodiversity.
Host: [calmly] Is there a risk this becomes symbolic, a token gesture cities make while ignoring larger structural harms to habitat?
Guest: That's a real risk. A dozen swift bricks mean very little if the surrounding wetland that supported the ecosystem for centuries gets paved over regardless.
Host: [encouraging] So this only matters within a much larger commitment?
Guest: Exactly right. Wild infrastructure isn't a substitute for genuine habitat preservation, merely a way of ensuring our denser cities remain slightly less hostile to what still lives in them.
Host: [seriously] What would you say to architects skeptical this is worth the added cost?
Guest: I'd say we've spent a century designing cities as though we were the only species with a legitimate claim to them, and that assumption has costs too.
Host: A thoughtful challenge to end on. Thank you, Sabina, for such a clear-eyed account of a field most of us knew nothing about until tonight.
Guest: Thank you for the genuinely good questions.
